📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

It has been revealed that advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

Sources indicate that the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

It has been revealed that A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

Recent findings suggest that in the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

It has been revealed that during totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

It has been revealed that an image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

Sources indicate that he photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

Industry observers note that the corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

Recent findings suggest that to observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most crucial processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Sources indicate that space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very swiftly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she notes, of solar eclipse photography.

Industry observers note that the European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

Sources indicate that when Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

According to recent reports, habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” claims Habbal.

In a recent development, capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

It has been revealed that to create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller indicates. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

In a recent development, since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

It has been revealed that the teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

According to recent reports, if you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

Sources indicate that on the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

It has been revealed that but even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” states Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

It has been revealed that as the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

Sources indicate that those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

In a recent development, around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller claims with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

Sources indicate that the optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

Industry observers note that with just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

Recent findings suggest that the crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

Recent findings suggest that “The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller states. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Apple Pay is a go-to feature for iPhone users when shopping in stores, online, and in apps. Apple recently declared four upcoming features that make Apple Pay even better. Here’s how they work, plus one major expansion that’s rolling out now.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

One of my favorite changes in iOS 27 is the redesigned Apple Pay checkout interface. The upcoming interface makes it much easier to switch between different cards during the checkout flow on websites and in apps.

According to recent reports, in the newly introduced design, you can easily swipe between cards on the main Apple Pay checkout screen. You can also tap on a card to view a grid of all your available Apple Pay cards.

The design also makes it easier to see information about individual cards, including rewards, balances, pay later options, and more.

Recent findings suggest that iOS 27 was released to everyone last week. You can revision in the Settings app on your iPhone.

Apple and American Express recently announced a newly introduced partnership that lets you pay with American Express rewards points.

Sources indicate that when shopping online or in apps with an American Express card, you’ll see a upcoming “Use Rewards” option alongside your available Membership Rewards points balance. You can apply points to cover all or part of your purchase, right in the Apple Pay checkout flow.

American Express points redeemed via Apple Pay are valued at 0.7 cents each. For example, this means 10,000 points can be redeemed for $70 applied towards your purchase.

In iOS 27, Apple is adding a fresh “Tap to Share” feature that integrates with Apple Pay on iPhone for in-store shopping.

This feature is an extension of Tap to Pay on iPhone. Apple explains:.

With just a tap, customers can connect to a participating merchant’s iPhone for a more personalized and faster in-store purchase experience that allows for secure sharing of information, such as email and other contact information, shipping address, loyalty rewards information, and more.

Customers will also be able to view the items in their basket in real time so they can keep track of what they’ve purchased and ensure all sales and discounts are properly applied.

When done, shoppers can complete the checkout on their iPhone using Apple Pay.

iPhone customers with select banks can manage their debit card balances directly in the Apple Pay interface. According to Apple, you’ll be able to use Apple Pay to add money to a supported debit card directly in Apple Wallet or when checking out.

This one isn’t really a latest feature developed by Apple. Instead, it’s something that should’ve happened years ago finally coming to fruition. Walmart has announced that it is finally starting to roll out support for Apple Pay. Apple Pay is also rolling out to Sam’s Club as part of this initiative.

As of November, Walmart’s roll out of Apple Pay across the United States is complete.

As Apple Pay continues to increase in popularity and prevalence among retailers, it’s great to see Apple continue to improve the experience. Personally, Apple Pay is my checkout payment method of choice basically everywhere I shop — whether that’s online or in store.

These are the best over-ear headphones I tested in 2025 (or ever, really). Right now, you can get the WH-1000XM6 headphones for $348 (originally $459.99), their lowest price ever during the early Black Friday sale from Amazon.

The XM6 headphones improve on what were already excellent headphones. Sony upped the count of microphones from eight to 12 when compared to the XM5, which improves more than just how well you sound to someone on a phone call. The microphones are used in almost all of its features, like ANC, Adaptive Sound Control, and the headphones' Ambient Sound mode. They hear your surroundings to adapt their features accordingly. If you switch from a noisy room to a quiet one, the XM6 can switch from ANC to "aware mode" (if you have Adaptive Sound Control on).

These headphones have a lot more features that you can nerd out on in their companion app. The audio quality is second to none, with the fully customizable EQ giving you plenty of options to get the sound how you like it. I really like being able to see what codec you're listening to in the app's main menu. That way, there's no guessing if you're getting the best audio quality or not. They will give you 30 hours of battery life with ANC on and 40 hours of juice with ANC off. There's an AUX (3.5mm) jack for wired listening, which is a nice touch for audiophiles who still rock iPod Classics (or is that just me?).

According to recent reports, the XM6s were not just the best headphones of 2025, but are still the best ones of 2026 and likely to be the best ones for years to come. For $348, you'll be securing the best for a record-low price.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can tell that Miranda Lambert is from Texas, but, until today, she’d never performed for her hometown football team — or anyone in the NFL, for that matter. Singing a medley of her classic hits (which she affectionately called “bangers and mash,” i.e., a mashup of her bangers), Lambert made her halftime show debut during the Thanksgiving Day matchup between the Dallas Cowboys and the Philadelphia Eagles at AT&T Stadium.

Recent findings suggest that following a pretaped introduction by Reba McEntire, who announced Lambert as the “most awarded artist in the history of the Academy of Country Music,” the Grammy-winning singer took the stage to perform “Snakeskin Boots” (sorry, no Ella Langley cameo), “Kerosene,” “Gunpowder & Lead,” “Mama’s Broken Heart,” and “Little Red Wagon.” Lambert was backed by her band, along with a string section wearing black cowboy hats to mirror that of the entertainer: Lambert, in a black hat, wore a black dress adorned with blue fames. She also received an assist from an army of Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, who delivered their choreographed routine as Lambert sang.

Recent findings suggest that lambert is a lifelong Cowboys fan who grew up in Lindale, Texas, about 80 miles east of Dallas. She now joins a cast of music’s biggest names as a halftime show veteran, including Beyoncé, Reba McEntire, LeAnn Rimes, Lainey Wilson, and Dolly Parton, who gave a memorable performance while wearing the iconic Dallas Cowboy Cheerleaders costume. Coined the “Salvation Army’s 30th Red Kettle Kickoff,” it was McEntire who performed at the inaugural broadcast, which kicks off the annual holiday fundraising drive. Lambert, true to form, unveiled her appearance from atop a longhorn bull. Trending Stories Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor Dead at 65 U2 Perform Dolly Parton's Final Recording During NFL Halftime Show ⁠Gérard Depardieu to Face Trial for Allegedly Raping Actress Charlotte ⁠Arnould Duran Duran’s Andy Taylor Was the Wildest of the Wild Boys.

“It’s my first time ever to do this,” Lambert stated during a visit to the Calm Down With Erin and Charissa podcast. “I’ve been doing this 23 years, and it’s my first halftime show ever. Isn’t that crazy? I don’t have a lot of firsts in my career at this point, but I was like okay, here we go.”.

It’s been a packed year for Lambert: her album Crisco came out in October, and she just took home a handful of CMA Awards for her work as producer and writer on Ella Langley’s Dandelion and song “Choosin’ Texas.” Next up is the Grammy Awards, where she is nominated seven times and could potentially make history if she wins Producer of the Year.

Soundcore's Q20i have dropped in price for Black Friday. They're comfortable, lightweight and sound great for the price, while also offering ANC.

It has been revealed that sound, ANC, comfort, styling. These cans have it all. The venerable Beats Studio Pro hit different when they're $200 off MSRP. Solid ANC? Check. A cool, stylish look? Check. Good sound quality? That's a royal flush, baby.

Recent findings suggest that bose might have replaced the QuietComfort headphones with an also reduced pair, but at this price, these are Bose headphones to go for. Excellent ANC for the price, a comfortable fit, and increasingly-rare-these-days physical controls.

The Nothing Headphone (1) can help you live out your sci-fi dreams while offering solid customizable sound and a great control scheme. Not bad for a Black Friday deal.

Recent findings suggest that the Momentum 4 have a reputation of being a little... boring. If, that is, you consider some of the best-sounding headphones for the price and 60 hours of battery life boring. I don't — and neither does this massive $120 saving on the Sennheiser Momentum 4.

Sony's XM6 weigh very little and sound excellent — and now you can get them for $100 off. As you'll see in our Sony WH-1000XM6 review, they offer excellent noise cancellation, improved call quality over prior models, and an epic 30 hours of battery life.

It has been revealed that pure. Class. That's how I'd describe the Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3. And I'd know, because I own and use a set of them on a near daily basis at home. In a recent development, the Samsung S90H OLED TV is a winning 2026 release from Samsung, delivering impressively vibrant yet natural colors and striking contrast. An upgraded version of the S90F, with better glare protection and brighter SDR brightness, it has been praised as one of the most versatile OLED TVs, especially for daytime viewing. Right now, a 55-inch Samsung S90H OLED TV is $400 off on Amazon at a record low of $1,197.99 (originally $1,597.99) for Black Friday. It’s worth noting that the other sizes are also discounted, with the 77-inch model 29% off.

In a recent development, while it has identical pixel-level contrast and wide viewing angles compared to the S90F, the major upgrade here is a matte-like screen, previously only seen on Samsung’s pricier models like the S95 series, bringing an extra perk and better reflection control for those with sunny media rooms. Contrast and color accuracy are highlights on this model, as is shadow detail.

In a recent development, the S90H offers four HDMI 2.1 inputs and supports refresh rates up to 165Hz with a compatible PC, up from the S90F’s 144Hz. It also supports VRR, FreeSync Premium Pro, G-SYNC, and ALLM. Like its predecessor, it’s powered by the NQ4 AI Gen3 processor for picture and audio processing. Its 40W, 2.1-channel speaker system supports Dolby Atmos, although neither TV supports Dolby Vision.

Sources indicate that if you’re looking for a well-equipped OLED at a mid-range price, the discounted 55-inch Samsung S90H is worth considering, especially if you’re a PC gamer or watch in a room prone to glare. It offers a stronger feature set than the S85H without requiring the jump to the more expensive S95H. Just compare the S90F’s current price before buying, particularly if movie nights in a dark room are your priority.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted.

The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler claims that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.

In a recent development, I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.

But the most frightening aspect of it is separate folders for individual victims containing all of the information needed for identity theft.

Fowler told Wired that this data appears to have been obtained through advanced malware.

The “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler notes, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims […] that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.

There’s no information about the specific sources of the data, but it seems likely to be aggregated from a range of data breaches. Fowler contacted the hosting tech giant to have the database removed, but it’s not known how many people may have had access to it.

The best protection is to use a password manager like Apple’s Passwords app to ensure you have strong, unique passwords for each individual website and service you use, with two-factor authentication enabled wherever possible. When given the choice of 2FA code delivery, you should always opt for an authenticator app rather than a text message to protect yourself against SIM-swap attacks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you want the most portable way to listen to music on the go, then the best earbuds are a fantastic way to do it. They're tiny, often comfortable, and offer noise cancellation to keep the sounds of the outside world at bay.

In a recent development, at the moment, the AirPods Pro 3 take the crown. But we've spent hundreds of hours testing earbuds to find out which are the best around if you want more than just Apple's offering. They come at a range of different price points to suit any budget, too.

It has been revealed that each entry on the list has a quick read section, giving you a brief overview of the buds, followed by longer reviews so that you can get a better idea of how they perform. So let's get straight into it. These are the best wireless earbuds you can buy right now.

We've spent 20 years testing the best earbuds (and the worst; you don't know until they're in your ears) to help you find your next set of portable audio companions.

The expertise comes from a few places, including our expert reviewers Erin Bashford and Nikita Achanta, who lead our audio testing. Then there's me, Tammy Rodgers, and I've been testing audio equipment for over half a decade, including a time as Tom's Guide's Audio Editor.

Before any earbuds make their way to this guide, here's how we put them through their paces to make sure we only recommend sets we truly believe in and would use ourselves.

It has been revealed that when you're looking for new earbuds, there's a whole range of terminology brands will use to talk about specs and performance. To make things a bit easier, these are the most common terms that come up, and what they mean for you.

According to recent reports, most earbuds come with Active Noise Cancellation (ANC). It uses audio magic and some very clever algorithms to quiet the outside world and make your commute more manageable.

It has been revealed that the earbuds have mics on the outside to pick up external noise. As this passes into your ear, the earbuds generate an opposing frequency to cancel the sound before you hear it. Sometimes this can change the sound of your music, so we'll report when the ANC is either too weak or too invasive.

Industry observers note that the EQ, or equalization, allows you to customize the way the earbuds sound. Usually, this means a series of sliders or dials in the companion smartphone app for adjusting the bass, mids or treble. Some manufacturers give you preset EQ options, which save you from getting lost in sliders or graphs.

Sources indicate that these are the different sounds that make up your music. You'll generally see them divided into three simple sections: the lows, the mids, and the highs. The lows are the bass frequencies. Think bass guitars and kick drums. You want them to be impactful and low.

Recent findings suggest that the mids are the main parts of your music, like vocals, guitars, and synths. Because they're so crucial, you want them to be thick and wide. Finally, the highs are cymbals and other higher sounds. These should be crisp and clear.

Tammy is one of Tom's Guide's Buying Guide Editors. She also spends a great deal of her time testing the best earbuds, evaluating them for sound, ANC, comfort and battery life. She's always got at least three pairs of earbuds to choose from at her desk.

Erin is a proud music nerd and needs the best earbuds around. Whether it's eardrum-shedding nu-metal or tranquil folk, she'll listen to it. If a pair of earbuds has awesome sound quality, bouncy ANC and are comfortable? It's an immediate recommendation, regardless of price or brand.

Sources indicate that as a music nerd, Nikita is always listening to music. As a reviews writer, she tests earbuds by pushing battery life to the limit and analyzing performance across various genres to answer the question: Are they good value for money? She listens to music almost throughout the day and plays guitar and bass, so she knows how to determine whether a pair of buds reproduces sound well.

According to recent reports, why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Recent findings suggest that the AirPods Pro 3 are the latest version of Apple's popular flagship earbuds. The stem-like design remains, but you get better battery life, an improved fit and more detailed sound. This makes them a worthy upgrade from the AirPods Pro 2, and the gold standard for wireless earbuds. Plus, the Pro 3 have a built-in heart rate monitor and Live Translation (if you have a compatible iPhone).

In a recent development, the AirPods Pro 2 were excellent, but soon aged out compared to the competition. Now, the AirPods Pro 3 have arrived to conquer all and lay waste to Sony and Bose. And, despite a couple of minor flaws, they're at the moment the best wireless earbuds you can buy right now.

It has been revealed that these are the very best earbuds that Apple has ever made. They've got some key updates over the previous model, for one. There's the extended battery life of eight hours, improved sound quality, and superior noise canceling to keep the noise of your commute at bay.

Those upgrades have materialized in a pair of buds that stun in sound and make sure that your office is a whole lot more tolerable when you're getting on with your day. They lose out to the Sony and Bose due to a lack of codec support for Android devices, but there really is nothing better if you're an iPhone user.

Industry observers note that the AirPods Pro 3 improve on the old model in the sound department. They've still got Apple's more neutral sound signature built in, but find more detail and extra bass depth than the older pair.

In a recent development, they've got a very solid soundstage as well. They're on par with the Sony buds, and better than the Bose alternatives — although there are still options out there that sound better.

Industry observers note that spatial Audio for movies with an Apple TV is still a great way to watch your content, and just as easy to connect up. It works well for music as well, especially when you listen to your music on Apple Music.

Sources indicate that the buds have been shrunk this time around, and as a result, have a very comfortable fit. The silicone eartips have been infused with foam for a softer and more comfortable finish, and they mold better to the inner part of your ear.

Recent findings suggest that that means you can wear them for extended periods of time. The sweat and water resistance means you won't have to worry about wearing them when you go to work out, either, hitting an IP57 rating this time around.

The AirPods Pro have always had 'good enough' ANC; powerful but not exceptional. But that changed with the Pro 3, which now almost compete with the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2, but don't quite beat out Bose's buds.

Industry observers note that still, it's very good and blocks out all the major noises of your commute or your busy office. It's on par with the Sony WF-1000XM6 — both are excellent noise-canceling options.

According to recent reports, transparency mode is very good as well, and boosts the battery life by another couple of hours. Nice.

Industry observers note that there isn't an app for the AirPods Pro 3, but you can easily adjust their settings from the iPhone settings menu. There, you'll find all their features along with options to upgrade the firmware and change the sound.

Sources indicate that although you can pair the AirPods Pro 3 to an Android phone, I wouldn't really recommend it. You get the bare minimum on a non-Apple phone; a wireless connection. You can't adjust settings, so I'd only suggest the AirPods with an Android phone if you're in a bind.

Much like on the Apple Watch, the battery life for the AirPods has remained stuck for years, allowing the competition to lead ahead. The AirPods 3 Pro buck the trend and, for once, increase the per-bud battery life up to eight hours of ANC listening.

That's a two-hour increase and puts them almost in line with the Sony and Bose sets. If you switch over to the transparency mode, you get 10 hours of battery life, more than pretty much anything else at their price point. That also means you can use the new Live Translation feature for longer.

Recent findings suggest that the Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds boast excellent sound quality, customizable EQ, and great battery life. Noise cancellation excels, and the design is also great. These are a highly recommended upgrade for superior quiet and sound control.

When following up on a highly successful pair of earbuds, there are a couple of things you do. First, you make things better — more features, better sound quality. Then you improve the design — make the fit better, improve the looks.

Sources indicate that that’s the WF-1000XM6, Sony’s follow-up to the WF-1000XM5. The AirPods of this generation make a better case for your money if you wield an iPhone, but the XM6 are great for just about everyone else. Just like their predecessor, they’re a fantastic all-rounder, with great specs, sound and ANC.

Sources indicate that our four-star review highlights that they’re not entirely perfect. The fresh case design is a bit odd and makes fitting them into a pocket a chore, and they’re more expensive than the previous model, but those are our only major criticisms.

Sources indicate that the sound quality is, as you might expect for something from the WF-1000X series, very good, with support for LDAC. Sony’s excellent DSEE Extreme audio upscaler is here as well, and works a treat. The ANC boasts a massive improvement, too, although Bose still has Sony beat for out-and-out noise performance.

They’re a wonderful pair of comfortable buds with plenty of battery life — there’s little more you could ask for, apart from a discount.

Sources indicate that they may seem on the expensive side, but the upgrades in sound performance make them totally worth it. Sony is known for a warmer sound profile on their headphones, and these are a total joy to listen to.

They are only made better by using the personalized EQ settings on the earbuds, and there’s seriously no genre that these buds can’t cope with.

Your favorite songs will sound a lot more detailed, and it’s really awesome to get a studio sound from earbuds instead of having to rely on studio headphones to do the job.

These earbuds are superbly comfortable, and you get a bunch of different eartip options in the box to get the best seal and best security. You can do a fit test to make sure everything fits.

I can wear these buds for hours at a time — they’re seriously comfortable, and they’re lightweight so they never weigh me down.

According to recent reports, ANC differs depending on personal experience with these buds. My own experience was amazing, and I couldn’t fault them at all. They made a long travel day on a plane, train, and bus completely silent.

It has been revealed that however, another one of my colleagues who tried them out was still able to hear the sounds of traffic moving around. I think it’s all about the eartip fit, so this is an extremely crucial process to complete.

If you buy this set, just make sure you use the Optimal Earbud Tips feature in the Sound Connect App to get the best fit, and ensure your ANC is working properly.

Recent findings suggest that the Sound Connect app is one of the most user-friendly I’ve tried. Once you get the hang of things and organize the app to suit the settings you need to use the most, it’s incredibly handy and makes using the earbuds so much better.

The app is where you do all the earbud fit tests and personalized EQ tests to make the overall experience with the buds so much better.

You get eight hours of battery per bud with ANC and 24 hours with the charging case. This is pretty standard and matches up with Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 and the Sony WF-1000XM5.

The A100 SE are all about sound — pure and simple. There's no feature bloat, no extra AI things, just a pair of great-sounding earbuds with epic battery life. The ANC has fallen behind the competition a little this time around, but they're a great pick for a fantastic price.

In a recent development, the first Cambridge A100 are some of my favorite wireless earbuds — and the SE version are no different. They come in at a price that doesn’t break the bank and offer some of the best sound quality around. For sub-$150, they sound better than buds that cost twice as much — there’s a reason we constantly compare them to the AirPods Pro 3 and others in the review.

They’re refined and classy in their sound, as befits a legacy British Hi-Fi brand. The soundstage is expansive and well layered, and vocals shine. Erin loved the dynamism and vibrancy in her review, noting the accuracy and faithfulness of their representation. High praise indeed.

Recent findings suggest that we had no problems with the comfort as well, and wore them extensively during the testing period. The case is compact and well-shaped (perfect for fitting them into a tighter pocket), and the app is useful and well laid out, though simplistic.

There are just a couple of problems. The ANC isn’t quite up there with other options at a similar price, and the Dolby Atmos mode is, like, bad. But beyond those two bugbears, the A100 SE are the perfect successor to some of our favorite earbuds and a top-notch value pick.

Cambridge has fired a warning shot at just about every other audio manufacturer with the A100 SE. The first model sounded good, but these sound even better. We love how dynamic and clear the buds sound, and the seven-band custom EQ means you can really dial them in.

Industry observers note that they sound better even than more expensive earbuds, and take the fight to options that cost $100-$150 more. That’s the focus of the buds: excellent sound, forget the frills.

According to recent reports, there’s warmth here, but it doesn’t overshadow the rest of the sound. Everything is still very clear and expansive, with solid instrument separation. We’re significant fans of the sound.

We scored the buds well for comfort, thanks to their smooth shape and range of different eartips. For the most part, we were able to wear them for long periods without them getting uncomfortable. We didn’t want to rip them out after the workday.

In a recent development, but those with small ears might struggle a little more. These aren’t small buds, and for one tester, they pressed on some parts of their ear. They weren’t uncomfortable, but they knew they were there.

The ANC isn’t going to win them any awards. It’s fine and blocks out some noise, but it’s not as all-encompassing as other options available. If you’re looking for something that blocks out everything, then you might want to think about Sony’s similarly priced options.

Still, if ANC isn’t a priority but you still want some noise blocking, then you won’t find anything to complain about — and the noise-canceling compromise is worth making for that excellent sound.

According to recent reports, cambridge’s app is fine, but we did have some problems with some of the features. It became a little buggy at times, with some features not working as they should. A quick restart fixed the issue, but it’s still worth mentioning.

What we really liked, however, was the complete omission of extra feature bloat. There’s everything you might need — an EQ, ANC controls, and that surround mode — but there’s nothing extra. No AI feature, no voice control thing, just what you actually need when using the buds. That’s refreshing.

Battery life is a particular strength of Cambridge's headphones and earbuds. Here, we’ve got 39 hours on tap, 10 hours of bud life. That’s more than just about anything else out there, including buds that cost a whole lot more. It even takes some over-ear headphones to task, and they generally have buds beat for staying power.

It has been revealed that everything charges up quickly, and we found that the battery figures matched up to expectations when we did all of our testing. If you want something that lasts a long time, the A100 SE are a great option.

According to recent reports, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the fitness lover's dream. A very comfortable, secure fit so that they stay in place no matter how you move around, and great sound quality to power your workouts. The built-in heart rate monitor is a great cherry on top.

Now, I'll be the first to admit that I'm not a fitness expert — but I sure am an earbuds expert. From my review, our fitness expert Nick said:"I genuinely believe that the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are outstanding sports headphones and would be top of my list for people who need an earhook to keep their buds in place during runs and other workouts.".

For all kinds of exercise, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are an excellent earbud option for everyone.

It has been revealed that while not high-fidelity, there's a rhythmic energy to the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 that's infectious. They've got some great bass presence, as you might expect, but they're also good in the upper register too.

According to recent reports, they fall down slightly in the mid-range, with a dip in the upper mid-range. That can take the edge off guitars and other instruments, although R&B listeners aren't going to notice too much.

Thanks to their excellent earhook, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 aren't going anywhere when you do your exercise. It can be a challenge to get them in place, but they're very stable once in.

The buds themselves are comfortable for long periods of wear as well, thanks to the silicone eartip options that you get in the box. The fit finder in the app is good as well, so that you can dial them in perfectly.

Sources indicate that the transparency modes work well enough, although I found that voices occasionally became fuzzy or tricky to hear depending on the surrounding noise. A shame, but not a deal breaker.

In a recent development, both methods let you control the ANC and dial in the EQ settings. They're simple, but they work well enough. Android users might find the occasional crash, however.

Industry observers note that the battery life of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 is exemplary. They feature 10 hours of battery life in the buds themselves, beating out many other options on this list.

That's perfect for long-distance runners and cyclists, or gym-goers who want something that will take them to the gym, last through their exercise, and then take them home again. We found those battery life claims were true in our review. Pop them in the charging case for 45 hours of staying power.

In a recent development, improving on almost every metric compared to the original model (except battery), the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 are an in-ear noise-canceling triumph. Boosts to ANC and sound quality make them an even better buy than the first model, and the price hasn't increased to match the improved performance.

Recent findings suggest that the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds were my favorite release of 2024, and the Gen 2 are now my favorite of 2026. They remain the very best way to listen to music without disruption when you're traveling. That busy train carriage? Silenced. The office? Quietened completely. With that signature orchestral swell, you're in your own world, free to listen to your tunes.

According to recent reports, sound is much better this time around, although you'll still want to adjust the EQ in the Bose app. And you'll be listening comfortably for their entire 6-hour battery life thanks to their incredibly comfortable fit.

They sound great out of the box, but these improvements make them sound even better.

In a recent development, there's also Immersive Audio, Bose's spatial audio setting. Some like its ability to make music sound much larger, but I find it thins out key frequencies. It also tanks the battery by two hours, making them last an even shorter time.

Sources indicate that yeah, they're still some of the most comfortable buds you can buy. I've been able to wear them for hours and hours at a time without the need to adjust the fit or take them out for a break — they're a lovely thing to have in your ears.

According to recent reports, it's all down to the fitting options. There are loads of different silicone tips, and the fit is further improved by the rubber fins you can attach to the edge. They're secure as well, so they won't fall out should you get headbanging or dancing.

The ANC is the best around — there's nothing that comes close. That's high praise given how good the previous model was at keeping out unwanted sounds, but Bose has somehow made it even better. It's a bit like magic.

In a recent development, you can choose different levels for the noise canceling, but I prefer to leave it on the top level. That way, I don't have to worry about any noise making its way through at all, and I can enjoy my music to the max.

Bose's app is one of the better options around. It's very well laid out, and everything is clearly labeled so that you don't get confused. It even shows you what's playing, although I'm not entirely sure how useful that feature is.

In a recent development, it's where you'll find all of the EQ options, noise control, and different sound modes. I particularly like how the app knows what color your buds are — and even lets you name them.

It has been revealed that battery life remains a weak point in the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2's armor. We've still only got six hours' worth of life here, which pales in comparison to some of the competition.

According to recent reports, the WF-1000XM6 last for eight hours, a whole two hours more than the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. You can't even turn the ANC off to boost the battery life — six hours is all you're going to get.

The Noble Fokus Amadeus are all about one thing and one thing only — their sound quality. Sound quality that blows just about everything else you can buy out of the water. Their ANC is very good, and they're very comfortable, but you buy these for their sound quality.

According to recent reports, the Noble Fokus Amadeus are not cheap. They're more than the AirPods Pro 3, and $50 more than the XM6 and the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds. They're not the most expensive earbuds around, but you should be ready to shell out if you want a pair.

And you will want a pair, because they've dethroned other excellent-sounding earbuds with their incredibly well-rounded sound signature that dishes out masterful amounts of detail while providing plenty of low-end punch.

For the price, this is about as close to wired earbuds as you're going to get. The crisp detail is utterly sublime, their mids are fat and juicy, and the bass is tight, controlled, and impactful. An audiophile's wireless dream, one might say, and the upcoming earbud sound quality standard that all else must be measured against.

In a recent development, the price means they're out of reach for many consumers, but as I discovered in my testing, they're well worth their higher price thanks to a very good all-round package. The battery is good, and the ANC matches up — there's very little to get sad about here.

According to recent reports, the absolute best thing about the Noble Fokus Amadeus is their sound profile. Thanks to the Audiodo profile in the app it means they sound amazing for everyone too, catering the sound for specific hearing needs.

It has been revealed that there are details in my tracks I'd not heard for a while thanks to the impressive detail, and the mids bring plenty of body to listening. The bass kicks and barks with impressive control, notably adding more for drum and bass in particular.

The sound is effortlessly spaced apart for a wide soundstage, and the instruments are very well separated. They sound better than absolutely everything on this list — they're hard to get hold of, but it's worth every single effort when you do.

Recent findings suggest that the Amadeus come with a range of different fitting options in the box for a very comfortable fit. They're more shaped and molded than other options as well, making them easier to wear for longer periods of time.

My favorite fitting options are the flanged tips because they not only improve the sound and the ANC, but they stay in place better than the other options.

While not quite as good as the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2, the ANC is still very good, especially if you opt to use the included flanged tips. It blocks out plenty of noise, focusing on low-end sounds like bus engines.

In a recent development, transparency mode is nice and natural as well, and makes it easier to talk to shop clerks and bus drivers without needing to take buds out of your ears. There's perhaps a little more noise than some might like, but it's otherwise very good.

In a recent development, the Noble Fokus app is very simple and lacks some of the more in-depth modes and settings of some of the competition. It's very easy to use, though, and offers everything you actually need.

There's the Audiodo sound customization, as well as a very in-depth EQ to really dial the sound in to your preferred listening curve. You can also change the noise-canceling mode and adjust the volume. Beyond that, there's not much else. At least there's a nice picture of your buds.

Battery life is very solid in the Fokus Amadeus. The buds last for eight hours with the ANC turned on, and 12 hours if you turn the ANC off. They charge promptly in the case, which provides a total of 42 hours of charge. That's amongst the very best battery life on the list.

Wireless charging is the cherry on top, and a 10-minute quick charge for two hours of use is a nice bonus too.

CMF's latest pair of budget buds are sub-$50 heroes. They pack in loads of premium features, like great customization and even a form of spatial audio. They sound great, fit well, and come in a range of different colors. What's not to like?

It has been revealed that this is a spot that’s likely to be occupied by CMF for some time — the brand's budget buds are just that much better than everyone else's. For just $50 (and often less thanks to significant price drops during deal events), you get earbuds that feel like they’re worth a whole lot more.

Recent findings suggest that CMF has packed in a whole range of great features. There’s sound customization from Dirac, which generally deals with premium Hi-Fi equipment. You get a form of spatial audio to make your music sound bigger, and there’s even great ANC to keep the outside world at bay.

Sources indicate that the sound is the most impressive thing here, though. They sound like a pair of buds that cost loads more, and once you’ve gone through the Dirac sound tuning, there’s very little better for under $100. Premium buds — low price.

Thanks to CMF’s use of Dirac, the CMF Buds 2 sound excellent. While the core sound is very good, with plenty of bass for impact and revealing detail for interest, the EQ settings kick things up a notch. We’ve described it as “breathing fresh life into your songs” — and you’d be hard-pressed to find something at this price that sounds better.

They’re great for a wide range of genres as a result. We spun up everything from the heaviest of metal to breezy folk and classical, and the buds didn’t skip a beat. They’re as meaty as they are delicate — extremely impressive considering the price.

It has been revealed that there’s nothing else that sounds like this at the low price point at which they sit. Even without Dirac, they’re impressive — although you’ll want to run the tuning engine to get the most out of them possible.

Thanks to a multitude of fitting options in the box and a great bud design, the CMF Buds 2 are very comfortable. There are three different sizes, and we found that the ‘small’ size option was perfect for even very small ears.

There are comfier buds out there, but we had little problem wearing them all day during our testing. More expensive buds might feel slightly nicer in the ear, but these still feel great for the price.

Industry observers note that you can’t expect Bose-level ANC for $50, but you’ll be immediately impressed by the noise-canceling packed into the CMF Buds 2. It does a very good job of keeping the outside world at bay, with some very impressive noise blocking.

In a recent development, the transparency mode is good too, making it easy to hear what's going on without a robotic edge. They cut down slightly with the ANC during calls — while your voice will be clear, your call partner will be able to hear everything going on around you.

It has been revealed that the Nothing X app is excellent. It's super simple to navigate, with easy access to all the features in the buds. There’s a home screen, and then various menus that are clearly labelled. It’s a must-install if you pick up the CMF Buds 2.

Industry observers note that this is where you find the Dirac tuning menu, as well as other settings. Those include the ANC settings, fit test, spatial audio, and touch control settings.

In a recent development, 11 hours of use in the buds is very solid indeed, and our testing showed no reason to dispute CMF's claims. The case contains 55 hours of use, so you can charge the buds about four times from empty. This is good battery life for buds, better than even some of the more premium options.

Samsung's latest buds bring a less AirPods-like case design and excellent sound quality to the table. Some settings and options are locked off for everyone but Galaxy device users, but they're a great option for the Samsung faithful.

Not one to miss out on a good earbud battle, Samsung’s Galaxy Buds 4 Pro bring a whole host of features to the Samsung crowd who want something that seamlessly integrates with their phone.

Sources indicate that they sound great, and Samsung’s audio upscaling tech is almost as good as Sony’s for improving weaker streams from the likes of Spotify and YouTube Music. That looks like the place Samsung has put the most work into the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro, improving massively over the older model.

Not quite as much work seems to have gone into the battery life, unfortunately. There are only around seven hours on tap with ANC turned on, which lags behind the key competition like the eight hours of the AirPods Pro 3. Still, you get more charge in the case at 30 hours.

Industry observers note that samsung has also packed in some very solid ANC, with loads of clever modes if you wield a Galaxy handset. That’s where their true value lies. There are a bunch of features that only Samsung consumers will appreciate, like AI translation that only works with Galaxy phones.

According to recent reports, if you’re a Galaxy phone user, then the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro were likely already on your shortlist. Thanks to our testing, we can tell you that they’re a great pair of buds that’ll pair with your device perfectly.

Recent findings suggest that “Overall, the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro sound utterly divine” is how Erin finished off the sound portion of the buds review. That’s thanks to rich bass, excellent mids, and great vocals, giving you a top-notch audio experience.

Detail heads might prefer the slightly tighter AirPods or Sony WF-1000XM6, but these sound better than the likes of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. Their AI sound enhancement works great with lower-quality streams as well.

It has been revealed that thanks to some solid shaping, the Buds 4 Pro are comfortable to wear for long periods of time. There are plenty of fitting options in the box as well to make sure that you’ll find the best fit for you, no matter what shape your ear canals are.

Some with smaller ears might find their slightly larger bodies tighter, but it’s not enough to make them in any way uncomfortable.

The noise canceling is excellent, blocking out all the noise that we could throw at them. They perform about the same as the AirPods and Sony competition, making for more relaxing journeys while wearing them.

Transparency mode is also good, and doesn’t make any of the incoming noise sound robotic. The ANC performance might not be quite as impressive as the Bose buds, but it’s more than a match for the Sony and Apple alternatives.

Some of the headline features, like the AI settings and call enhancement, are only available for Galaxy S23 models and newer. The buds use the Samsung settings menu itself rather than a dedicated app on these devices, and it works well.

Recent findings suggest that there is a Samsung app for other devices, and it's fine. You can control the ANC and other settings, and update the firmware. Still, there are better app experiences for non-Galaxy users, like the Sony and Bose apps.

Battery life is fine. It’s not as good as the eight hours you get from the AirPods or the Sony WF buds, but the seven hours on tap is more than enough to get you through the day. The 30 hours in the charging case, though, make up for the slightly lacking battery life of the buds.

Not every pair of earbuds we test can land on the best list — otherwise, this would just be a list of earbuds that are available to buy. But some are still pretty good and worth considering if you need more options.

Thanks to some key upgrades (mostly in the sound department), the AirPods 5 are a great pair of earbuds, especially with the latest lower price compared to the AirPods 4. The battery life just isn't good enough, however, and compatibility with Android remains an glitch that holds them back from a full-chested recommendation.

It has been revealed that the EarFun Air Pro 4 bring some excellent features at a bargain price. For a lot less than $100, you get solid ANC, great sound, and a very comfortable fit. They last for ages thanks to their 7.5-hour per-bud battery life, and support loads of hi-res codecs so that your music always sounds its very best.

Read our full EarFun Air Pro 4 review.

Sources indicate that the Cambridge Audio Melomania M100 are wonderful earbuds with impeccable sound and a monstrous 52-hour battery life. But the ANC isn't as effective as we'd like, and the case is large and cumbersome to carry around.

Read our full Cambridge Audio Melomania M100 review.

In a recent development, sony's WF-C710N are well-priced buds that bring some great specs to the table and don't cost the earth. Their ANC is solid, and the sound is very good. We found them comfortable to wear for long periods of time. Whether you like the transparent blue design will probably help you decide if these are right for you.

Read our full Sony WF-C710N review.

The Liberty 5 Pro Max are Soundcore's first entry into the premium earbud space. It is largely successful, with good sound and solid ANC. But at this price, the AirPods Pro 3 or Sony WF-1000XM6 are better value for immersive audio with ANC.

Read our full Soundcore Anker Liberty 5 Pro Max review.

Before we make a recommendation about any pair of wireless earbuds, we want to make sure that we've put them through their paces. It helps us find out how good they'll be when you find them in your hands, and makes sure that we can pen our informative, buying advice-packed reviews.

It has been revealed that it's all work — no fun. Listening to our favorite music for hours on end to test the sound, taking the earbuds out and about on day trips to test their long-term comfort and ANC algorithm. In all seriousness, we put a lot of effort into making sure that you'll be happy with a purchase you make after reading our buying guides and reviews.

Here are the key factors in our testing and how we evaluate each pair of earbuds that falls across our desks.

Earbuds are going to be jammed directly into your ear holes, so one of the most vital things that we test is how comfortable they are over long periods of time, and how difficult it is to dial in the fit. How many bud bits do you get in the box, and are they easy to fit on the buds? Are they loose? Are there extra fitting options like earhooks?

In a recent development, to find out, we put the buds through their paces. We try out a range of the tips that come with the budsto find the perfect fit that makes the ANC excellent and sound good. After all, if they don't seal well inside of your ear, you're not going to get the best out of your buds. We report our findings, like how easy it was to get the perfect fit, and how comfy they are when dialed in.

In a recent development, then we test their long-term comfort. That means wearing them for hours during a work day, so that we can see how they feel when they're worn for hours on end. If they start impacting certain pressure points in the ear, we'll notice, and it'll go into our review. We're looking for earbuds that can't be felt during wear, so that you forget you're wearing them.

This is my favorite thing to test. Hours and hours of my favorite tunes played into my ears while I work, and I don't have to make excuses to my boss about why I need to be doing it. Excellent news. When we test the audio quality of a pair of buds, we play the Tom's Guide testing playlist on Qobuz so that we can get a good picture of how they sound with some top-quality hi-res tracks to put them through their paces.

Recent findings suggest that we listen at first in a quieter environment so that we can get an idea of how they sound in a vacuum without the ANC to cause potential problems. We compare the earbuds to the sound profiles of those in the best list above, and then we write down our findings for the full review.

Then, we take the earbuds out with the ANC to see if it changes the sound. It might all sound like we're having fun, but there is a point to it all. It gives us a clear picture of the buds' performance in an everyday use case, so that we can see how they'll serve you if you decide you'd like to buy a pair.

Pretty much every pair of earbuds that you can buy today comes with some form of ANC (unless you buy some of the very cheapest ones at the very end of a lengthy Amazon search, you madman), and we want to make sure that it performs well in a variety of use cases.

In a recent development, how do we do it? By taking the earbuds with us wherever we go. That could mean on all our daily commutes, to see if they perform well on the train, or out for hikes so we can see how well they handle normal atmospheric noise. Maybe we're going on a flight — then we can test how well they handle loud engines and crying children.

Once we've thoroughly tested how much noise they block, we also test the transparency modes when we go to buy our tickets or a bag of candies from the grocery store. We look out for how clear the voice of our conversation partner is, and whether they're audible through any other noise. We're also looking out for the quality of the audio that's being pumped in. Is it too loud? Again, we note down our findings for the review.

Finally, we want to make sure that the ANC doesn't change the sound of the music too much. After all, you want your music to sound great, and if the ANC changes things too much, it can create annoying sonic issues.

Industry observers note that given that your earbuds are often going to pull double duty as a form of hands-free calling system, we want to ensure that they're going to be good at it. We make a whole bunch of calls to check things out.

According to recent reports, we're looking out for a couple of different things. First of all, we want to make sure that we can hear our call partner well, and that they're coming through clearly. We listen out for clarity and judge whether we can hear them properly throughout the duration of the call, and whether their voice sounds natural.

Then we ask our call partners how we sound. Can they hear us properly, or do the noises of our environment make it hard to hear what we're saying? We note down our findings, and then we report back on them in our review to give you an idea of how they'll perform if you want to take (or make) a call.

We know that manufacturers sometimes have a habit of overestimating their battery life figures. To make sure that you're getting the best information possible, we spend the time testing the battery life claims and whether they ring true. We listen to the buds for hours on end, and count how many hours we used them before they needed to go back into their case. We do this with ANC turned on and with the volume at a comfortable level.

According to recent reports, for charging cases and very long-lasting buds, we extrapolate battery data in a different way. We measure how long we've used them, and then compare that with how much life we've got left. This gives us a good picture of how the battery is going to last in the long run, and whether you'll get those rated claims.

According to recent reports, hopefully, we've managed to curate a list of wireless earbuds that hit the mark for you. But if you're still not sure how to choose between them, these are some additional pointers.

What do you want out of your buds?

There are as many reasons to buy earbuds as there are earbuds themselves. You need to work out what you're looking for first and foremost — it's why I've divided the list up into the most notable headline features.

Recent findings suggest that do you want the best sound, and would you be willing to give up some battery life and pay a bit more for it? If not, then you should go for the best earbuds overall, but if you don't mind some compromise, then you should go for the best-sounding earbuds.

According to recent reports, it's important to make a list of the features that are most important to you, and then work out from there which of the earbuds on the list fit those criteria the best. After all, what might be the best for one person might not be the best for you.

Do you want headphones or earbuds?

Sources indicate that if you're looking for the most compact, easily transported audio device around, then the best earbuds are probably going to be right for you. But there are a couple of things to remember: they're going to live inside your ears, and not everyone likes the feeling of in-ears after longer periods of listening.

If you'd prefer something more comfortable for longer periods of wear that offers more battery life, and potentially better audio quality, you should consider some of the best wireless headphones. They might cost a bit more, but you might be more comfortable.

Industry observers note that repairability is becoming ever more vital, as we try to find new ways to lengthen the life of our devices, but also look after the planet that we call home. Repairing products is great for both, and it's important to consider it when buying new tech.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, earbuds are one of those products that are extremely rarely user-repairable. Thanks to their size and the amount of tech that companies have to pack into their buds, it's generally impossible to make the insides accessible to you or me.

Sources indicate that not all is lost, however — some manufacturers do offer some form of repair service, so you don't have to worry if your buds stop working. But this is still pretty rare, so if this is a priority for you, it's worth picking up a pair of the Fairphone Fairbuds 2.

Sources indicate that there are seven user-repairable components; they cost less than $100 and come in two colors. Tom's Guide Managing Editor James Frew rated the first generation, but they weren't available in the U.S. That all changed with the Fairbuds 2, which you can buy directly from Fairphone.

In a recent development, I talk about this on our best headphones list, but I think it's worth reiterating here. It's easy to get hooked on frequency response graphs and numbers, and think you're getting a surefire cheat code to finding the best-sounding earbuds.

You'll spot them as a pair of numbers in spec lists, like "15 Hz-22 kHz." The first number is how low the earbuds can go, and the second is how high they can go.

According to recent reports, you might think that finding a pair with the greatest frequency range is going to net you a pair of excellent-sounding earbuds. While that can be true, it's not worth seeking out. Just because a pair of earbuds can go really low doesn't mean they're good at replicating those frequencies, and neither does it tell you about what's going on in the music itself.

There's only one way to really tell how good a pair of earbuds is — and that's to give them a listen. Or, of course, you could read one of our excellent and informative earbuds reviews.
