  • Perfect for artists of all skill levels, the Ohuhu Hilo markers come in packs of 48 or 72 and are an affordable option compared to rivals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re an artist and you use social media, you’ve probably heard about Ohuhu by now. This brand quickly made a name for itself simply because they offered high-quality alcohol based markers at prices that undercut competitors. I have to admit that I turned my nose up at them at first; I didn’t believe they could be as good as the markers I already owned when they cost so much less.

In a recent development, in short, I should have listened to Ohuhu’s supporters. I was able to try out both the Honolulu 2S alcohol markers, and my first ever set of acrylics with the Hilo brush tip acrylic paint markers. I was blown away by both.

Perfect for artists of all skill levels, the Ohuhu Hilo markers come in packs of 48 or 72 and are an affordable option compared to rivals. They have a soft brush tip and can be layered up on the page for an opaque finish.

It has been revealed that ohuhu's Honolulu 2S alcohol markers come in a huge range of colors, with 320 markers in the biggest set! These dual-ended markers feature a brush and a chisel tip. While you'll need to watch out for bleed through, they produce a beautiful and smooth finish.

It has been revealed that I started off with the Hilo acrylic markers. These markers have a single, soft and flexible brush tip, and you can right now get either a set of 48 or a set of 72 at Amazon. I was excited to see how they would perform, so I stuck a Holiday movie on, sat back and got out a coloring book to test them out.

As soon as the pen touched the page, I was immediately struck by the vibrancy of the colors and the opacity of the ink. Sure, the first sections of color I filled in were the blacks, but I couldn’t believe my eyes when the numbers almost disappeared under the acrylic ink. Some of the colors are less effective at this than others — but layer the ink up a few times, and you’ll have one gorgeously clean looking coloring page!

According to recent reports, as for the experience of using them, the soft tips give plenty of control. They felt incredibly smooth to use across gentle curves and coloring medium to large areas was easy and comfortable. These acrylic markers give you the ability to go over and redo areas you’re not happy with if you accidentally color over something you didn’t want to, which is a huge bonus.

Another positive under this set’s belt is the carrying case.The design is so cheerful that it immediately put a smile on my face the first time I saw it, and it honestly still does every time I open it. And compared to other name brand acrylic markers, they’re significantly cheaper — the 72 set works out to around 70 cents per marker at the Black Friday sale price.

According to recent reports, there are some downsides to contend with. When it came to coloring small, detailed areas... I pretty much had to forget about staying within the lines. I struggled to achieve fine pointed shapes and found that the ink pooled into circular shapes every time I attempted them. I also had concerns with streaky ink, and my coloring paper pilled in certain spots, too.

This is my first time using acrylic markers, so I’m willing to acknowledge all these problems could come down to my lack of skills. I’m going to keep using them and see if I can improve my technique and layer up more to combat the streaks. The pilling probably isn’t going away until I get a coloring book with higher quality paper, though.

It has been revealed that next up, I tried the Honolulu 2S alcohol based markers. You get more color options here as the sets come in packs of 24 all the way up to 320; and these markers have a dual tip. One side has a brush tip, and the other is a chisel tip.

Compared to the Hilo's, the Honolulu 2S’s brush tip is firmer and stiffer. Even though the Hilo brush tip felt great, I liked the Honolulu 2S’s firmer brush tip even more, and found it easier to control when coloring detailed areas and sharp points. It still handles curves just as well, and the chisel tip comes in handy for filling large areas too. I fell in love with alcohol-based markers years back because they produce a beautiful, non-streaky finish. The Honolulu 2S markers absolutely live up to that and looked fantastic on the page.

According to recent reports, however, using alcohol based inks comes with more of a learning curve. I started off filling in a large black area on the page once again, and was very impressed that the marker didn’t bleed much at all. However, other colors like the dark blue and gray didn’t fare so well, and bled right over the lines.

According to recent reports, the bleed can be mitigated by using paper made specifically for alcohol markers, but you don’t have that option if you want to color in a specific coloring book. It took an hour or two for me to get used to it, but I eventually learned to leave plenty of space while filling areas in to account for the bleed.

As well as bleeding over the lines, I also had to watch out for the ink bleeding through the paper — Ohuhu provides a plastic sheet to place under your work to avoid staining the next page in your sketchbook. The ink in the Honolulu 2S markers was clearly visible on the back side of the paper I colored on (seen on the left of the image below,) but none got through to the next page. Meanwhile, the back side of the page I colored with the Hilo markers (seen on the right below) was completely clean.

It has been revealed that if you’re a budding artist, I highly recommend picking up a set of Ohuhu markers. The Hilo acrylic markers are the ones for you if you want the most vibrancy, and are also great if you want to have the option to redo areas if you’re not happy with them. Meanwhile, the Honolulu 2S markers stand out for their enormous color selection, excellent brush tip and super-smooth finish.

Industry observers note that these markers are cheaper than the big brands, and are even better value when discounted. Grab them while you can!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar highlights how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

In a recent development, in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar highlights how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

It has been revealed that in the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

Recent findings suggest that in the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also indicates how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

AI agents now control part of DeepMind's compute for Gemini experiments

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (235 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: The-decoder

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google Deepmind lets AI agents run experiments on their own for the next Gemini model.
  • According to Kavukcuoglu, AI agents control part of the compute themselves to run experiments, though the lab is still far from full recursive self-improvement.
  • Industry observers note that kavukcuoglu also points to limits.

Google Deepmind lets AI agents run experiments on their own for the next Gemini model. On the organization's podcast, VP of Research Koray Kavukcuoglu, who leads Gemini development, frames this as part of a strategic shift at the lab. Rather than running separate teams for specialized projects like AlphaFold and nuclear fusion, Deepmind now relies on a single general-purpose algorithm for both science and products, he says. Each Gemini generation, he adds, is a hand-built one-off rather than a fixed architecture, while parallel teams work on its successors.

According to Kavukcuoglu, AI agents control part of the compute themselves to run experiments, though the lab is still far from full recursive self-improvement. As a safety measure, Deepmind doesn't reward the agents' internal thought streams ("Chain of Thought") during training, he claims, so their intentions stay unfiltered and reviewable in natural language before they act.

Industry observers note that kavukcuoglu also points to limits. Today's AI can depict physical processes such as fluid flows and collisions with visual accuracy, he says, but doesn't understand them precisely. No test can show when models will close those gaps and reach artificial general intelligence (AGI), he argues, because no benchmark captures the core of intelligence. In his view, AGI won't begin until useful everyday products earn enough trust for people to hand decisions over to them, the way they would when working with other people.AdAd.

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

In a recent development, the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

In a recent development, “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

The screen highlights my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

Recent findings suggest that for Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” indicates Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

It has been revealed that in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Industry observers note that yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

In a recent development, the N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

According to recent reports, sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team highlighted me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

In a recent development, remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

Industry observers note that this system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga indicates. “It was just significant enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Industry observers note that dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In Upcoming York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

Sources indicate that but telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics tech giant XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

Industry observers note that “The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” claims Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson indicates. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

According to recent reports, nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

Industry observers note that in 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Sources indicate that noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more vital than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell notes. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” notes neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Sources indicate that medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, states experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

According to recent reports, and connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu notes.

According to recent reports, medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” notes neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra indicates, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

It has been revealed that if smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Sources indicate that neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell claims. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in fresh funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

According to recent reports, sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he claims. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

Industry observers note that the steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga notes they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How rapidly are doctors picking up on this fresh technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

In a recent development, these ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person organization into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

Back in July, PrismML claimed its roughly 4 GB, 1-bit Bonsai 27B was the first AI model of its size to run on an iPhone. Now PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an patch to the model it introduced in September.

The startup also drew attention when CEO Babak Hassibi told CNBC that Apple was evaluating its technology, as we reported at the time.

It has been revealed that the upcoming model is based on Qwen3.8 27B and keeps the same 5.9 GB footprint in its most compact format. This time, PrismML focused on helping the model handle longer tasks, including figuring out what to do when a tool returns an unexpected result or a step fails.

Bonsai 2.5 improved on six of the seven benchmarks PrismML highlights. Its SWE-bench Verified coding score rose from 60.8 to 75.6, while its AppWorld tool-use score jumped from 51.2 to 90.5. LiveCodeBench v6 dipped from 83.8 to 83.0.

According to recent reports, what could that look like on a Mac? A coding assistant could inspect a private project, make a change, run the tests, and use the results to revise its fix. A document app could summarize a folder of sensitive files while keeping the processing on the device.

Industry observers note that prismML says Bonsai 2.5 runs on Mac, iPhone, and iPad through MLX. Its Apple silicon package is about 8.9 GB, and the model card walks through setup on a Mac. The weights are available for free under Apache 2.0.

For a closer look at how the model was compressed and tested, read PrismML’s technical white paper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gerald R. Molen, an Academy Award-winning producer behind Steven Spielberg‘s Amblin Entertainment, has died. He was 91.

It has been revealed that on Sunday, Molen’s niece Rachel Pullan announced that he died earlier that day. “This morning my great uncle, Gerald R. Molen, passed on to join my great grandma and his dear wife Pat on the other side of the veil,” she wrote on Instagram. “I am so happy for him, and also so very sad.

“Uncle Jerry was a man of great moral character and high integrity. He started doing work, moving set pieces and driving at a movie studio, and worked his way up to the position of producer. He worked on many great films, including Jurassic Park, Schindler’s List (for which he won the Oscar for best production), Rain Man, Minority Report and The Other Side of Heaven, just to name a few. He held to his beliefs and standards and industry where that was often difficult to do. Minority Report is rated PG-13 because Jerry told Steven Spielberg he would only do the movie if it wasn’t rated R, and Spielberg made it happen—it was worth it to him to have Jerry be his producer. Jerry influenced millions of people, both by his example and his contributions to the telling of brilliant stories in film.” Related Stories Casting Steven Spielberg Sets Adaptation Of 'The Heart In Winter' As Next Film At Focus With Jessie Buckley, Cillian Murphy And Mark Rylance Starring And Paul Thomas Anderson Adapting The Script News In Newly introduced Book, Joe Biden's National Security Aide Brett McGurk Describes Jeffrey Katzenberg & Steven Spielberg Advising POTUS On Major Gaza Speech.

Pullan added, “I’m glad I was able to go see Uncle Jerry a couple of times in the last few years before he passed. I will be watching Jurassic Park in his honor tonight. It was definitely one of his personal favorites stash as evidenced by the number of dinosaur she had on every surface in his house. Love you, Uncle Jerry— say hi to great Grandma for me.” Watch on Deadline.

In a recent development, born Jan. 6, 1935 in Great Falls, Montana, Gerald Robert Molen grew up in North Hollywood after his family relocated there.

In a recent development, in 1985, Molen began working with Spielberg as a unit production manager on The Color Purple, before going on to produce his movies Hook (1991), Jurassic Park (1993) and Schindler’s List (1993), which earned them the Best Picture Oscar. They also worked together on The Lost World: Jurassic Park (1997), Amistad (1997), Minority Report (2002) and Catch Me If You Can (2002).

Latest Update: An annoying ‘mistake’ in macOS was actually prep for the latest MacBook Pro

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (482 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, you may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail.
  • According to recent reports, I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail.
  • It turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, you may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail. The reason for this has now become clear, and Apple has done something both fun and clever in macOS 27 to resolve it ….

According to recent reports, I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail. Developer Norbert Heger pointed out this is because Apple changed the radius of the corners without changing the grabbable area.

It turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it. The window expects this click to happen in an area of 19 × 19 pixels, located near the window corner. If the window had no rounded corners at all, 62% of that area would lie inside the window. But due to the huge corner radius in Tahoe, most of it – about 75% – now lies outside the window.

At the time, the radius change itself looked like an inexplicable mistake on Apple’s part, and the manufacturer did revert it. However, Macworld’s Michael Simon appears to have discovered the reason for the original change.

The new rounder corners on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR are basically a perfect match for the macOS 26 radii.

It has been revealed that so if you move a window to the corner of the new machine, it would fit perfectly. However, since Apple reverted the corner radius, it would no longer do so. The firm solved this by a clever UI transition.

What’s happening there is Golden Gate’s 20-point corner radius is subtly and gradually expanding when It approaches the bottom corner of the screen to match the exact corner of the display, which is much larger. I can’t be certain it’s exactly 26-point, but it sure looks like it to me. The effect is incredible. I’ve watched it like 20 times and I can barely see it changing, yet when it reaches the corner it’s perfectly expanded to match.

You can see this illustrated by a GIF in the Macworld piece. While the original change annoyed me, Apple’s solution is the perfect example of the company sweating the details.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

It has been revealed that this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

It has been revealed that this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

#211566. Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1230 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Techstackups ↗ Open Full Page

Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1230 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techstackups

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, on 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms.
  • Industry observers note that read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels.
  • If you've built an email assistant on the Gmail API, or you run a coding agent with a Google Workspace plugin, you have about two months to work out which side of the rule you're on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest of Workspace through those servers.

Industry observers note that read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels. It can't send a message, reply, forward, or change a draft after creating it. Those tools exist, but Google's quota page notes they "require partner access and aren't generally available".

If you've built an email assistant on the Gmail API, or you run a coding agent with a Google Workspace plugin, you have about two months to work out which side of the rule you're on.

The newly introduced Workspace AI Tools Addendum to the Google APIs Terms of Service puts it in one sentence:.

The GWS Access Tool must use a Google MCP where the GWS Access Tool is or is driven by an AI Agent, an AI Harness or an AI model or service employing an AI model.

In a recent development, the next sentence forbids disguising an agent to avoid the classification. Breaking either lets Google "restrict or remove the GWS Access Tool's access" or suspend your account.

There's a technical side too. From the same date, agents that call the REST APIs directly are held to Standard-tier quotas, whatever tier the project has paid for. REST keeps working for them, slowly and in breach of the terms.

It has been revealed that apps that don't involve AI carry on as before. A nightly backup job, a CRM sync or a deterministic script on its own OAuth client is, in Google's words, "not affected by this change".

The addendum also adds data rules that matter to anyone building an agent with memory:.

In a recent development, the 30-day cap is the one product teams will feel. An assistant that builds a long-term index of your inbox to answer questions about last year's contracts has to rebuild it monthly or drop it.

Sources indicate that coverage is uneven. Docs, Slides and Tasks are close to everything the REST API offers. Gmail and Drive are much thinner.

Sources indicate that the Gmail gap is the one that breaks real workflows. An agent that drafts a reply, gets feedback from you and revises it before you hit send can't do the revision step. It has to create a second draft and leave the first one behind.

Drive's gap is similar: an agent can create a report but can't move it into the right folder or share it with the team.

In a recent development, google hasn't said who qualifies for partner access or when the partner-only Gmail tools will reach everyone. The effect is already visible, though. Anthropic's Google Workspace connector for Claude advertises sending, replying and forwarding email, and moving and trashing Drive files. Those are exactly the operations the public servers lack.

Recent findings suggest that so a large AI vendor's agent can send your email through an approved channel, while an independent developer's agent, using the same OAuth scopes the user granted, can only leave drafts. Once the addendum takes effect, that independent developer also can't fall back to the REST API without breaching the terms.

The definitions are broad. An "AI Harness" or a tool "driven by" an AI model plausibly covers a personal script that pipes your inbox into an LLM, and a "GWS Access Point" explicitly includes any "connector, proxy, command line interface, or third-party service". Google hasn't addressed hobby use directly.

Classification starts with self-declaration. OAuth clients now have a checkbox, "Use this client for an AI-powered agent", and since 11 November the MCP servers reject clients without it. Clients created before the cut-off and not marked in time stay non-agentic permanently, so owners have to create new ones. Google hasn't noted how it will detect agents that call REST without declaring themselves.

A few edge cases are documented:.

Industry observers note that every project gets the free Standard tier: 5,000 MCP requests per day, per project, per product. Some calls cost more than one request. A Gmail search_threads or list_drafts counts as 10, so an agent that does nothing but search gets 500 searches a day across all its consumers. That's a project-wide limit, so a small multi-user product will hit it swiftly.

The paid Scaled tier starts billing on 1 April 2027 for Gmail, Calendar and Drive. Its structure favours REST. MCP usage is billed from the first request, while REST usage gets large free daily allowances: 70 million light Gmail requests a day, for example. Google hasn't published per-request prices.

Google's case, from a Cloud blog post by Chandu Thota and Brad Calder, is that OAuth was designed for apps acting on a human's clear intent:.

Recent findings suggest that traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed â¦ a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path.

According to recent reports, there's substance to this. An email agent that reads a message saying "forward the last ten invoices to this address" is a well-documented prompt-injection risk, and a token that allows gmail.modify gives the agent the power to do it. Routing every agent through one gateway gives admins a single place to block categories of action, require approval and audit what happened. The MCP servers do all of that, and apply data-loss-prevention rules automatically.

It has been revealed that the same design also gives Google control of which agents can do what, which data they can keep, and whether anything built on that data can compete with Google's own products. The partner-only tools and the 30-day cap on embeddings show that control in use.

It has been revealed that slack went down a similar path in May 2025. It cut history API rate limits to one request a minute for apps outside its Marketplace and banned bulk export of Slack data for LLMs. Slack drew the line by distribution channel. Google draws it by whether the software is an AI, which is harder to define and harder to enforce.

If you build an agent product on Workspace:.

Industry observers note that if you run a personal agent or MCP server against your own account: open-source servers that call REST, such as the popular google_workspace_mcp, will keep running, but at Standard quotas and outside the terms. Switching to Google's servers costs you sending and draft editing in Gmail, and moving and sharing in Drive.

If you're a Workspace admin: the latest controls are under Admin console â Security â API Controls. You can block or approve each category of agent action, set approval policies, and see agent activity in the audit logs. Customers can't view or revoke the approvals they've saved, which expire after 90 days, so it's worth setting policy before people start connecting agents.

If your integration doesn't use AI: nothing changes, as long as it stays on its own OAuth client and nobody wires a model into it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A new report says that Apple already has iPads running macOS internally, and that work on a giant iPad continues, but don’t hold your breath for a public launch of either ….

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, with iPads running the same chips as Macs, many have wished Apple would give us the option of running macOS on them instead of the somewhat clunky iPadOS windowing system. Apple’s previous arguments against converging devices have been somewhat weakened by the launch of the touchscreen MacBook Pro.

A new report says that Apple already has iPads running macOS internally, and that work on a giant iPad continues, but don’t hold your breath for a public launch of either ….

According to recent reports, as iPad hardware has grown more powerful over the years, the software has struggled to keep up. We saw split-screen capabilities first, with full windowing finally coming to the devices in iPadOS 26 last year.

The UI is still rather clunky compared to macOS, however, leading a significant number of people to wish that Apple simply offered the option of using the more powerful operating system on its tablet devices.

I would be comfortable with 11" and 13" devices running macOS. Actually, I don’t require them to run macOS itself, but I do need them to run macOS apps. I wish the iPad could match a MacBook’s productivity. Running macOS on an iPad seems like a reasonable idea. The MacBook Air is now the better price choice, while those needing a powerhouse will always choose a MacBook Pro or Studio.

According to recent reports, some suggest that running macOS on iPad would reduce Mac sales, but I disagree. I own a nearly full-spec MacBook Pro 16" and expect to keep a machine like that, yet I also purchased a MacBook Air for lighter travel. I would prefer an iPad over the Air, but I cannot choose it because it lacks the apps I require. If it supported them, I would buy the iPad Pro with all accessories, and Apple would gain more revenue from me. I appreciate the concept of owning an iPad, but at the moment it lacks the value needed to justify paying more for a device that simply does less than a MacBook Air.

In a podcast Q&A, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman claims that Apple is already doing this internally, but there’s no sign of any plans to make it available outside the tech giant.

Industry observers note that apple has iPads internally running macOS, and they’ve had that for some time. The fact that they have the underlying architecture of Apple Silicon that’s the same on the iPad and the Mac gives them the flexibility in order to test these types of things.

In terms if they’re actually going to do it – would they bring macOS to the iPad itself – at this point I don’t think that’s going to happen anytime soon. I’ve checked into this and there’s no ongoing operating system project right now in terms of a brand new operating system for the iPad – there is no work being done to consumerize macOs on the iPad.

Gurman indicates Apple seems set to continue to make piecemeal changes over time to bring iPad capabilities closer to those of the Mac but is showing no signs of full convergence.

He reiterated that work on a long-rumored giant-sized folding iPad continues.

The other thing I want to say is that I’m really excited for this potential of Project J312. That is, this giant 19-inch, 20-inch foldable iPad. And it’s basically like a gigantic iPhone Duo with no display on the outside.

However, he says there’s no guarantee it will ever launch, saying the timings have already slipped from 2027 through 2028 to 2029, but both cost and yield complications may still kill the project. If it does launch, it’s expected to cost anywhere from $3,000 to $5,000.

Microsoft states China’s Salt Typhoon and North Korean hackers now use ARTEX

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft logo at the Microsoft Experience Center, New York.
  • In a recent development, state-backed hacking groups from China and North Korea, including Salt Typhoon, have added the AI attack framework ARTEX to their tools, Microsoft indicates.
  • Recent findings suggest that the list covers Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, two Chinese state groups, and Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet, which Microsoft tracks as North Korean.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft logo at the Microsoft Experience Center, New York.

In a recent development, state-backed hacking groups from China and North Korea, including Salt Typhoon, have added the AI attack framework ARTEX to their tools, Microsoft indicates. Microsoft Threat Intelligence named the groups in a report published on Wednesday.

Recent findings suggest that the list covers Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, two Chinese state groups, and Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet, which Microsoft tracks as North Korean. Two more clusters, Storm-0940 and Storm-3358, are also on it. Microsoft states state-sponsored and financially motivated hackers use ARTEX to speed up network scans, credential attacks, and attacks on web apps.

“Depending on the threat actor’s configuration and the target’s defenses, ARTEX can advance from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access to a target organization in a matter of minutes,” Microsoft wrote.

The report landed hours after US media tied ARTEX to the hack of three US spy agencies, as Jonathan Greig reported for The Record.

In a recent development, US agencies believe Salt Typhoon breached at least nine telecoms groups in 2024, The Record noted. That hack allegedly reached phones used by Donald Trump and JD Vance. A US House report later remarked Chinese carriers were still inside American phone networks.

Crystal Typhoon is newer. It was first seen in late 2023 and goes after government networks and critical infrastructure through edge devices and firewalls, TechRadar reported.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft had already linked Storm-0940 to the ConnectWise supply chain attack. The upcoming report adds numbers from its campaigns. In one, Microsoft logged more than 151,000 failed sign-ins, peaking at 2,900 a minute. In several intrusions, the attackers had privileged access less than three hours after they first went after a target.

In another case, an AI agent went from searching GitHub for client secrets to taking data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

A GitHub user called Autumn-27 published ARTEX as open-source code with a Chinese interface in July. The developer took it down in October, but other developers kept publishing their own versions. This month, the Chinese security firm ThreatBook claimed ownership and started selling access to “ARTEX Pro”.

According to recent reports, the attacker sets the targets. One AI model breaks the job into goals. A planner agent then hands short tasks to worker agents with a real shell and hacking tools. A reporter agent writes up what worked. ARTEX can run on almost any large language model, including ones stripped of their guardrails. That means no single AI provider’s safety controls can stop it, Microsoft says.

The FBI warned about ARTEX earlier this month.

“ARTEX does not introduce new attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques,” Microsoft wrote.

Attackers can change the tool’s IP addresses and user agent strings, so blocking those alone will not work. The steadiest sign is behaviour: many varied requests in a short burst, and quick moves to the next step. ARTEX does nothing to hide that activity by default.

Sources indicate that microsoft also suggests honeypots, tarpits, and fake wins. A fake win shows the agent false proof that its job is done, so it stops. It recommends rate limits, phishing-resistant multifactor sign-in, and replacing any secret that leaks into code. The report also points customers to Microsoft’s own products, including Defender XDR and its Perception security agents.

In iOS 27.3, which will launch to all people next month, Apple has design changes coming to four popular apps: Health, Calendar, Safari, and Music.

The Health app gets the biggest design changes.

As seen above, Health introduces brand upcoming Insights, Longevity, and Browse tabs that replace the previous options and include a variety of fresh UI elements like a top navigation row, personalized prompts and coaching, educational videos, and a lot more.

Calendar also now highlights the year at the top of the screen next to the current month, and has updated the ‘Today’ button to show the current date instead.

In a recent development, safari introduces an optional new design for tabs: Vertical Tabs. You can enable these inside Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Safari for a different approach to tabs across iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Here’s an example of vertical tabs on iPhone Duo.

Vertical Tabs won’t be for everyone, but they’ve proven popular in other browsers, so it’s great to see Safari add the option.

Song artwork is now able to break the constraints of a square and blend seamlessly into the scrolling lyrics view. Here are examples from Beta Profiles on X:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Official Grand Theft Auto VI artwork featuring Jason and Lucia.

Rockstar Games staff in the UK have voted against recognising a union, a week after the studio launched Grand Theft Auto VI. Three in four votes went against a recognition deal with the IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union. The Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB) unveiled the result on Thursday.

About 1,600 staff below director level could vote. Of those, 1,544 took part, a turnout of 93.2%, Chris Kerr reported for Vertical Slice, which broke the result. The ballot ran from 12 to 26 November.

In a recent development, the split was 75.3% against and 24.7% in favour across the Edinburgh, Leeds, Lincoln, Dundee, and London offices, GamesIndustry.biz reported. IGN put the count at 1,163 votes against and 381 for.

Industry observers note that A yes vote would have made the branch the largest recognised union in the UK games industry. It would have set up formal talks on pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, and pensions. Staff would also have had a say on HR policies and on how Rockstar uses generative AI, Vertical Slice reported.

The union already exists, and staff can still join it. The result means management does not have to hold regular meetings with its representatives. Under UK law, the union cannot apply for recognition again for three years, according to GamesIndustry.biz.

“Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues,” the IWGB mentioned in a statement.

Sources indicate that the union said the result “isn’t a sign to retreat”. It will keep pushing for pay transparency, contractual overtime pay, and protections against AI and layoffs.

“This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong,” Jennifer Kolbe, Rockstar’s head of publishing, stated in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that the vote follows a long dispute. In October 2025, Rockstar fired more than 30 staff, all IWGB members. The studio indicates they leaked confidential information in a Discord channel. The union says those talks were protected union activity and accuses Rockstar of union busting.

According to recent reports, the fired workers took the case to an employment tribunal in Glasgow, which heard closing arguments on 19 November. Their lawyers argued the sackings came soon after an informant said union membership was nearing 10% of staff. That is roughly the level needed to apply for recognition. Rockstar’s counsel told the tribunal the workers were “caught red-handed”, Wccftech reported. Judge Lucy Wiseman has not yet ruled.

The ballot overlapped with the biggest launch in Rockstar’s history. GTA VI made $3.79 billion in a record first day, after it tied Metacritic’s record with a 99. Take-Two has said the game was built without generative AI.

Signal’s Moxie Marlinspike claims AI safety is building mass surveillance

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that moxie Marlinspike, who built Signal, indicates the way AI companies police misuse is turning into the biggest mass surveillance system ever built.
  • “You’re building a machinery of mass surveillance that is larger and more efficient than any other mass surveillance machinery in history,” Marlinspike said.
  • Recent findings suggest that he described today’s approach as scoring everything consumers do for “badness” and sending the worst to human reviewers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that moxie Marlinspike, who built Signal, indicates the way AI companies police misuse is turning into the biggest mass surveillance system ever built. He wants the watching pointed at the AI models instead of the people using them, he told Tyler Cowen on Conversations with Tyler. The episode was recorded live at the Progress Conference on 10 October and published on Wednesday.

“You’re building a machinery of mass surveillance that is larger and more efficient than any other mass surveillance machinery in history,” Marlinspike said.

Recent findings suggest that he described today’s approach as scoring everything consumers do for “badness” and sending the worst to human reviewers. TNW reported in September that contractors read real ChatGPT conversations.

His alternative is to monitor whether the models themselves show bad tendencies. Labs would train narrow models that each spot one kind of behaviour, then use them to check the general models. Cowen asked whether using AI to watch AI really counts, pointing to the Hugging Face breach. Marlinspike noted it does.

In a recent development, chatbots invite confession because they feel private, Marlinspike said. In practice, chats end up in a data lake used for training and analysis.

“You feel like you’re having this conversation with this agent or assistant that gets to know you as your friend… but actually, it’s a huge group chat with many, many more people,” he said.

He runs Confer, a private AI chat service at confer.to. Only the user can read their chats, he mentioned, and he cannot. Claude and ChatGPT “are not operating private services,” he added, though he said the substantial labs could build one.

Asked whether the recent flood of AI maths results could break cryptography, Marlinspike answered: “I don’t know.”.

“If there is some result that just all of public-key cryptography doesn’t work anymore, then the whole internet is in trouble,” he stated.

In that worst case, nobody could trust software updates, websites or online banking. He also described milder outcomes, where some algorithms would only need larger keys. Moving to post-quantum encryption took about five years, he said, and a second switch would likely be faster.

On hacking, he expects a painful period before AI gets as good at patching flaws as at finding them. He put the wait at about a year. Cowen doubted that small cities could patch their systems that fast.

According to recent reports, marlinspike mentioned Signal knows almost nothing about its users. It cannot see their contacts, group names, profile names, searches, or stickers. WhatsApp uses the Signal protocol to encrypt messages, but much of that other data is not protected, he said. Signal recently moved to block AI agents from reading chats.

Cowen pushed back on privacy more broadly. He said face scans speed up airports and that CCTV cut murders in São Paulo. Marlinspike said it is hard to argue against a city with a murder problem. He still opposes airport face scanning and argued that law enforcement should stay imperfect.

Cowen also asked what the 2025 Pentagon group chat on Signal had done for the app.

“It made it all worth it for me,” Marlinspike noted.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adam Levy – Nov 26, 2026 at 12:15PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

The past six weeks have been tough for Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) and its shareholders. In October, growing concerns about how businesses will finance future build-outs for artificial intelligence (AI) started weighing on semiconductor stocks.

It has been revealed that in early November, the mid-term election results showed a clear rebuke of massive data centers and the potential for increased regulations to slow development. And, of course, Jensen Huang's affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two employees ultimately led to his temporary resignation, leaving Nvidia without a permanent CEO for 11 days.

It has been revealed that the end result is a stock well off its all-time high, despite having just reported third-quarter revenue and earnings growth that both exceeded 100%. CFO and interim-CEO Colette Kress said it's "business as usual" at Nvidia, painting an optimistic picture on the firm's earnings call. So, with the stock trading at a level rarely seen in the past year, should investors consider buying the stock? Warren Buffett's long-held investment philosophy can provide the answer to that question.

It has been revealed that warren Buffett. Image source: Getty Images.

Industry observers note that many investors might look at Nvidia's drop and think, "The market is fearful; I should get greedy." After all, Kress just increased her guidance for fiscal 2028 revenue growth from 70% to 75%. Wall Street analysts see Nvidia's earnings per share climbing above $16 next year. The stock trades at ridiculously low multiples.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

According to recent reports, while it's true that Buffett has long noted that one of the keys to his success as an investor is "to be greedy only when others are fearful," that's not the only requirement for a good investment. Buffett also only invested in stocks when he had a high degree of confidence in their future. If a company was deemed too difficult to understand or forecast, he stayed away.

"Investors should remember that their scorecard is not computed using Olympic-diving methods: Degree-of-difficulty doesn't count," Buffett wrote in his 1994 letter to Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.54%) (BRKB +0.37%) shareholders. "If you are right about a business whose value is largely dependent on a single key factor that is both easy to understand and enduring, the payoff is the same as if you had correctly analyzed an investment alternative characterized by many constantly shifting and complex variables.".

At this point, Nvidia's business is more like the latter than the former. Huang's actions and the potential repercussions leave many unanswered questions for investors. The high level of uncertainty about Nvidia's future explains why it trades at such a low multiple. It's not fear; it's a rational response to the recent events impacting the company.

There are a couple of alternatives to Nvidia stock trading at earnings multiples that aren't much higher than the chip leader.

Buffett himself initiated a position in Alphabet (GOOG -2.02%) (GOOGL -2.13%) in 2025. His thesis was based on the firm's ability to deploy huge sums of capital with a high return on investment. Specifically, Buffett was talking about its Google Cloud Platform and its data centers full of GPUs and custom silicon.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

Alphabet is well-positioned to deliver high returns on invested capital in Google Cloud because of its full-stack approach to AI. It designs the systems and chips in its data centers; it offers a full cloud platform for developers (not just infrastructure); it develops a frontier large language model; and it integrates AI capabilities across its products.

Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian remarked that its payback period for the average server in its data centers is just two years, and its custom Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) systems break even within half that time. With a useful life of six years and a good operating margin, that's an exceptional return on invested capital. That return on invested capital is set to climb as more spending shifts from data center shells to revenue-generating servers.

In a recent development, another company positioned to grow based on a single key factor is Broadcom (AVGO -0.07%). Broadcom is the leading custom AI accelerator design partner, the one Alphabet uses for most of its TPUs. Growing demand for custom silicon, which costs less up front than GPUs and offers better price-performance, should result in its AI chip revenue climbing faster than the competition's for years to come. Its lead is protected by its intellectual property and its close relationship with its foundry partner, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

While Nvidia right now trades around 16 times earnings expectations, Broadcom's stock price isn't much higher at 17 times forward earnings. Alphabet is more expensive at 21 times forward earnings, but it's arguably the least risky of the group, considering its digital advertising business remains a huge cash cow funding its growth.

#211544. Tech Report: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

Tech Report: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5197 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.
  • Data centers already use light in networking.
  • The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.

Data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

It has been revealed that the reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” indicates Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Sources indicate that optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys.

“I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” indicates Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in Fresh Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”.

Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Recent findings suggest that back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

According to recent reports, VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How substantial do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also vital to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law.
